1:
Clarke opens with the shape of the whole: the prophet is beaten and imprisoned for prophesying against Judah and Jerusalem, released the next day and denouncing judgment on the governor and his house and on the whole land, then bitterly complaining of the reproaches heaped on him and resolving in haste to speak no more, then professing trust and praising God for a deliverance, and finally regretting that he was ever born. He compares that last part to the complaint of Job, only milder and more dolorous, exciting pity rather than horror, and warns that the strong figures of eastern poetry are not always to be understood literally.

Who Pashur was takes some settling. Gill, Wesley and Henry agree he descended from the Immer who headed the sixteenth course of priests in the time of David, Henry using the description to distinguish him from another Pashur of the fifth course later in the book. Ellicott adds a possible identification with the father of a Gedaliah who opposed the prophet at a later date, notes that the name may mark the section rather than the immediate parent, and observes that it reappears after the captivity. On the office he is most careful: the word rendered governor is the higher title, given to the high priest and to a second priest, while the deputy is the lower; here the two are combined, perhaps to imply that Pashur held the full powers of the higher office as a deputy, though some invert the relation and make him chief warden. Keil and Delitzsch make the same distinction, that one word carries the idea of overseeing and the other the official standing of the overseer.

Calvin dwells on what made the blow a trial. It came not from the king or his courtiers but from a priest who had charge of the temple, of the same tribe and a colleague; and since the priests then in office had been appointed by God under the law, their authority was founded on his own inviolable decree, so that the prophet might well have been shaken. Calvin puts the questions in his mouth: what can be the purpose of God, who set priests of Levi over his temple and his people, and why does he not rule them by his Spirit and make them fit for their office, why suffer the temple and the sacred office to be profaned, or at the least not stretch out his hand to defend one who is also a priest and sincerely engaged in his calling? He points out that the law itself required death for whoever disobeyed the priests, and that not the prophet only but every true worshipper of the time was shaken by the trial. Henry makes the same point more briefly, that the greatest malignity against the prophets was found among those who professed sanctity and concern for the church, and that this priest persecuted the man he should have protected.

On the blow Ellicott notes that it is the first time the title of prophet is given him, apparently to sharpen the outrage; that other prophets had been killed under earlier kings but that none so far as we know had been put to an ignominious punishment like this, with one exception; and that the word used implies a blow struck with the hands of the priest rather than the legal scourging. Gill allows either that he struck him with fist or rod to stop his mouth and discredit him, or that he had him scourged by an officer. Clarke guesses at the place, something like a lock-up near the gate or a dungeon; Ellicott describes the instrument as one that held the body in a crooked and painful position, and leaves the prophet in it for the whole night at one of the most conspicuous points of the city.
3:
Calvin sets the scene. He supposes Pashur called other priests to examine the case, a specious pretence of not wishing to condemn hastily; the prophet says only that he was brought out of prison, from which we gather he was not dismissed but summoned to give a reason for his prophecy. What Calvin makes of it is a lesson in constancy. Such outrages, he says, are so bitter to ingenuous minds that they can hardly be borne; yet the prophet bore the buffetings and the stripes and the imprisonment patiently, and on coming out spoke more boldly than before, though he was still a captive and might have been thrown back and treated worse. Courage increases when a man has won and can safely insult his enemies; this was not that. Neither the wrong received nor the fear of new indignity deterred him, and Calvin makes the magnanimity a standard for all who serve God, that they should not feel shame nor grow soft nor be disheartened when the world treats them with contempt.

The new name is the point of the oracle. Clarke reads the old one as security on all sides, a name he had but not by divine appointment, and the new one as fear on every side, given by God because providence would place him in the circumstances it names. Wesley is careful that the meaning is not that men would stop calling him Pashur but that his condition would no longer answer a name signifying a flourishing priest. Ellicott adds that the new name is a quotation from a psalm, rightly rendered fear is round about, which the prophet had used before; he ventures the guess that the psalm had been his comfort through those night watches, and that he now spoke the words which had described the bitterness of the psalmist, feeling sure at last that they belonged to his persecutor rather than to himself. On the older name he thinks it scarcely necessary to hunt a special significance, though he reports the conjectural etymologies that have found in it joy round about, or freedom and deliverance. He also notes that the phrase became a kind of burden with the prophet, recurring in three later places, and that the word for fear is rare and found only once outside them.

The explanation of the name divides the readers. Gill offers two: either the conscience of Pashur would be so filled with terror at the coming judgment that he could not hide it, but would be seized with such tremblings that his familiar friends would shun his company and run from him; or the terror is the Chaldean army, which would frighten both him and the friends in whom he had placed his confidence, so that none could help. Ellicott presses further and prefers the first. We should have expected the terrors to gather round the persecutor from outside, he says, but the words go deeper: he is to be an object of self-loathing, the fears without intensifying the terror within and acting through him upon others, so that he is the centre from which terrors radiate as much as the point to which they converge. Calvin reaches much the same, that Pashur would become a spectacle to himself and to all others, unable however hardened to do otherwise than feel the divine vengeance.
5:
The word rendered strength is variously taken. Gill lists the fortifications and towers of one version, the riches of another, and the magazines and stores; Ellicott renders it simply the treasure or substance of the city; Calvin reports four ancient renderings, strength, substance, citadels and riches, and notes that the primary sense of the root is to be strong or firm, the word being sometimes taken metaphorically for wealth.

Calvin finds the sting in the next word. That what had been acquired with great labour should be given to plunder is the more grievous, since a man who becomes rich without labour, by inheritance and without toil, is not so distressed at losing it; whereas one who has obtained through a whole life of work what he expected would support him grieves far more, and is really distressed with anguish, when enemies come and strip him of everything. Labour, he says, is named here as it is elsewhere in scripture in order to amplify the evil. He also notes what the threat cost the prophet to utter, that Pashur was no doubt more exasperated by it, and takes that as the point: it was right to inflame the fury of the ungodly further, and though they raise a clamour a hundred times we must not desist from freely declaring the truth.

On the fate of Pashur himself the voices converge. Gill notes that he and his household should not escape whoever else did; Clarke says he shall suffer both for the false prophecies he delivered and for his insults to the prophet. Ellicott supplies the history, that the section of priests to which Pashur belonged is found in large numbers at Babylon in the later record, and that as a high official he would naturally be among the captives when all but the poorer sort were carried off; on the lies he had prophesied, which are not recorded, Ellicott infers that Pashur was among those who encouraged the people to resist the Chaldean army and to despise the warnings by holding out hope of an alliance with Egypt. Calvin makes him a proof rather than merely a victim, the whole family being led away as a spectacle so that all might know the impostor for what he was.

The burial raises a difficulty Calvin will not pass over. To die in Babylon and be buried there is announced as a punishment, yet the same prophet had elsewhere threatened that carcasses would be left to the birds and beasts, so that burial is reckoned among the favours of God. His answer is that the ungodly are not always punished alike: some are cast out unburied as unworthy of the common lot of humanity, others are buried but to a different purpose, and the weight here falls on the place. Babylon is set against the holy land, and whoever was buried in the land had even in death a pledge of the eternal inheritance.

Keil and Delitzsch look ahead from here and divide what follows into two: a complaint addressed to the Lord about the persecutions that the preaching of the word draws down on the prophet, which passes into a jubilant cry of hope, and then a cursing of the day of his birth.
7:
Ellicott marks an obvious break here: the narrative ends and a psalm of passionate complaint begins, and its position probably shows that whoever arranged the prophecies took the complaint to belong to this period, representing the thoughts of that night of shame which was the extreme point of apparent failure. This, the prophet seems to say, was the end of his calling and the fulfilment of the promise that he was set over the nations and that his enemies should not prevail. Gill places the words in the stocks or the prison and calls them a mixture of grace and corruption, a struggle between flesh and spirit under a temptation arising from the difficulties of the work. Henry says the same, and asks for the charity we would want ourselves: good men are but men at the best, and God is not extreme to mark what they say amiss, so neither should we be.

What the complaint means is the great question of the chapter. Calvin reports two readings he will not have. Some think the words were not spoken by the prophetic Spirit at all but uttered inconsiderately through a hasty impulse, as even the most eminent are sometimes carried away; others give a harsher account still, that the prophet had actually been deceived, on the analogy of a saying elsewhere about a prophet being deceived. Calvin holds instead that the language is ironical. The prophet assumes the character of his enemies, who boasted that he presumptuously foretold a ruin that would never come, and by repeating their charge he declares that God is the author of his doctrine and that nothing can be alleged against him which is not alleged against God; they contended in vain under the notion that they contended with a mortal man, for they openly made war on heaven. He was not deceived and did not think so, being fully satisfied as to himself and possessing a firm conviction of the truth he delivered. Clarke attacks the same problem through the translation, which he calls exceptionable and, taken as it stands, irreverent: the verb means to persuade or allure as well as to deceive, and the sense is that God persuaded him to go and prophesy; he quotes an old version giving thou leddest me aside. Ellicott prefers thou hast laid hold on me for the second clause, and reads the whole as the Lord appearing to the prophet as a hard taskmaster who had forced him against his will into a work from which he shrank and given him scorn as his only wage. Wesley makes it simply the overruling of the prophet contrary to his own inclinations at his call.

Gill sets out what the prophet might have thought himself deceived in. He had been told at his call that he should be set over nations and kingdoms to pull them down, which he understood of foreign nations and now found meant his own people, a reading Gill credits to an early authority; or the threatenings were not immediately executed, as in the case of Jonah; or he had been given reason to expect honour and ease and met nothing but disrespect and trouble; or he had been promised protection against his opposers and was now delivered into their hands and used in the most reproachful manner. Gill adds at once that all of this was a mistake.

Henry takes the derision as the substance of the wrong and allows the complaint as justly made to the one who sent him. He was ridiculed and laughed at, everything he said and did made a jest of, which cannot but grieve an ingenuous mind; and it was continual and universal, so that the greatest forgot their own gravity and the meanest forgot his.
8:
Ellicott makes a philological point the English hides: the two verbs are different words, the first a cry of complaint and the second of protest, so that from the beginning of his work until now he complains, and calls out against violence and spoil. Those had been the burden of his discourses, and the word so proclaimed had brought him only derision; he had been the champion of the rights of the people and they mocked him. Gill offers three senses for the crying, that he lifted his voice so all might hear, that he cried out of grief at the usage he met, or that he cried at what he was obliged to declare. Clarke and Wesley take the violence and spoil for the burden of the message given him.

Calvin explains why the preaching had to be loud. He first sets aside a reading he finds too frigid, that the prophet merely uttered complaints from the time he began to teach because he saw himself assailed. Nearer the truth, he thinks, are those who take it that the prophet cried out against outrage and plunder because all kinds of wickedness prevailed: he could not teach mildly, since the temper of the people forbade it and their wickedness compelled severity. Calvin turns this into a rule about tone. All the servants of God ought to consider what the state of the church requires; to cry aloud in tranquil times would be mad affectation, as many do who without thought and without reason always make a great cry; but when Satan is seen reigning we ought not to withhold or act as if under a truce, for where the war is open it is necessary to cry aloud.

The resolution to stop is unanimously read as inward. Gill and Wesley both insist he did not say it openly or even to his friends but in his heart, and Gill calls it a temptation that often besets a minister because of the usage he meets and the ill success of his ministry, one seen for what it is sooner or later; the prophet thought that since no credit was given him and God was dishonoured and no good done, it were better to be silent. Ellicott says the sense of a hopeless work destined to fail weighed on him and he would gladly have withdrawn. Clarke reads it as a hasty and disobedient resolution to renounce the office and go home, for which he then felt the stings of conscience and shame at his own weakness in not trusting the promise of God.

The fire is described in three ways. Keil and Delitzsch trace its anatomy: the word of God dwells in the heart, but from there it acts outward upon the whole organism like a fire shut up in the hollow of the bones, burning the marrow; the phrase shut up in my bones stands in apposition to the burning fire. Clarke says the word was in him as a raging fire and he was obliged to deliver it in order to be rid of the torture of suppressing it, and draws the moral that it is as dangerous to refuse to go when called as to run without a call. Ellicott recovers an echo the English loses: the words rendered I could not stay use the same verb as the prevailing of the earlier verse, so that God had prevailed against him and forced him to a work against his will, but he could not prevail against God. Calvin makes the confession itself the lesson, that the prophet was sore troubled to see the word of God made a derision and wished to withdraw, and that whenever such a thing comes into our minds we ought manfully to resist it.
10:
Ellicott finds the psalms again: the defaming of many and the fear on every side are both from a single verse of the psalm the prophet has been drawing on, and the new name he gave Pashur still rings in his ears and becomes the burden of his own cry. Gill describes the defaming as brought to him by friends, his character aspersed and false reports raised on all sides so that he could expect fresh trouble from one quarter or another; he notes that some would keep the new name untranslated and read the defaming of many such men as Pashur, and rejects it, since neither the accents nor the number will bear it. He also records a disagreement about the function of the verse, whether it gives the reason for the resolution to stop prophesying or an additional reason for going on, the prophet being pressed inwardly and provoked outwardly at once. Keil and Delitzsch treat the phrase as proverbial rather than particular, a set expression for a harassed condition full of terrors, and note that this prophet uses it often.

The conspiracy is reconstructed with some care. Ellicott corrects the English, which reads as though the persecutors addressed the prophet: the words are rather what they said to each other, do you report, encouraging one another to inform against him. Calvin fills in the mechanics. The chief men and the priests are the speakers, and since it did not suit their dignity to run about asking what the prophet had said, they sat still and sent others, saying go and report to us and we will report to the king. Worthless men run here and there and hunt out every little thing, then bring in their report, and from that the accusation is formed. Ellicott adds three touches from the vocabulary: the familiars are literally every man of my peace, those who greeted him with the customary salutation, which marks courtesy rather than intimacy; watching for his halting uses a word rendered adversity elsewhere; and the word for being enticed is the very word rendered deceived in the earlier complaint, so that the prophet in his bitterness saw the work of his enemies and the work of God as tending to the same result. Wesley puts their aim plainly, that they wanted nothing more than that he should say something they could make into a colourable accusation.

Then the complaint turns. Wesley describes the prophet as recovering out of his fit of passion and encouraging himself in God, whom he calls the mighty and terrible one, so declaring his faith both in the power to save and in the promise made at his call that God would be with him to deliver him. Ellicott hears the same movement as in the psalms, the prophet perplexed but not in despair, passing through deep waters and struggling out to a rock; and he shows the word terrible doing double duty, since God had promised to deliver him from the terrible ones and now shows himself more terrible than they, so that it is better to fall under their anger than under his. Calvin makes God the brazen wall set against every plot, whether perfidious friends entrap us privately or open enemies oppose us publicly, but attaches a condition: the power of God can do nothing to animate us unless we are firmly persuaded that he is on our side. On the last clauses Ellicott and Wesley agree in preferring because they have not dealt wisely to they shall not prosper, and in carrying the everlasting confusion through as one that shall never be forgotten. Clarke says only that by strong confidence in the strong God he was delivered from all his fears and enabled to go on comfortably with his work.
12:
Calvin makes this verse the proof of the one before it. Hypocrites often boast that God is their helper, but they falsely pretend his name; the evidence that the prophet did not is that he dared to make God the witness and judge of his own integrity. If we wish to plead the name of God against the artifices contrived against us, Calvin says, we must learn to offer ourselves to be tried by him, so that he may really examine our thoughts and feelings. And he adds the caution that gives the offer its weight: hypocrites will not hesitate to offer themselves for trial, because they have not considered that nothing is hid from God. There are many recesses in the heart of a man, and everything there has many wrappings and coverings; but God is a discerner of hearts, who proves the heart and the reins, the second word covering in that language all the hidden thoughts and feelings. Men gain nothing by acting fallaciously, since he penetrates to the inmost thoughts and distinguishes between the thoughts and the affections.

Gill reads the trying two ways, either that God tries the cause of the righteous and vindicates them, rights their wrongs and does them justice as the one who searches hearts and reins; or that he tries their faith and patience, their constancy and integrity, and on trial finds their affections real and their souls sincere. Ellicott notes only that the verse is almost word for word one used earlier in the book.

The last verse turns to praise, and everyone marks the turn. Gill says the prophet moves from prayer to praise and from confidence to a holy triumph, calling on his own soul and on others to join him; he reports an opinion that the summons is addressed to the saints then in Jerusalem, of whom there were doubtless some who had a regard for the prophet and wished him well. Ellicott gives the movement its shape, that heaviness had endured for a night and joy came in the morning, and compares the psalms in which a cry out of the depths ends in praise. Clarke observes that the deliverance was complete though the circumstances were not changed, so that the prophet exults in the divine protection and fears the face of no adversary. Calvin explains the summons: the favour was such that not he only should be thankful but all should join to celebrate it, so that thanks might be given by many. He also corrects two words, that the poor here does not mean one in low circumstances but one helpless and defenceless, and that the soul means the life. And he draws the lesson from the order of events, that when we are reduced to straits and seem rejected we should wait patiently, since without misery and distress going before we should never sufficiently acknowledge the power of God in preserving us.
14:
The sudden change from praise to cursing is the difficulty everyone must handle, and the answers differ. Henry asks whether blessing and cursing proceed from the same mouth, and answers that the prophet records this to his own shame as he recorded the previous verses to the glory of God; he takes it as a relation of the ferment he had been in while in the stocks, out of which faith had recovered him, rather than a new temptation afterwards, and adds that when grace has won it is good to remember the struggles of corruption, so that we may be ashamed of our folly and set a double guard on our spirits. Wesley reads it the same way, a repetition of a former passion rather than the product of his spirit at that moment. Gill allows either that it was spoken at another time and repeated here to show what distress he had been in, or that the two may be joined grammatically, the poor man delivered being the one who had said in his distress, cursed be the day. Clarke goes furthest: he believes the verses have got out of their place, which he conjectures to be between the eighth and ninth, transpositions in this prophet being frequent. Ellicott reports that some hold an accidental dislocation and would set these verses before the complaint, but himself prefers a distinct fragment of the same period placed here by the prophet or his editor.

Calvin rejects the new-temptation reading, which he says is how interpreters commonly untie the knot, and the levity it implies. He takes the whole passage as part of the thanksgiving: the prophet amplifies the deliverance just mentioned, having been brought back as from the lower regions, and recites what had happened earlier, as though he could not express the greatness of the favour until he made known how dreadful the agonies were in which he cursed his birthday and abhorred everything that should have moved him to praise. He was not only opposed by enemies, Calvin says, but distressed inwardly, carried against reason and judgment by turbulent emotions. And Calvin will not soften what follows: what is said here cannot be extenuated, and the prophet most grievously sinned in becoming calumnious toward God.

Ellicott traces the words to their source, the prophet turning in his suffering to the language in which the great representative of sufferers had cursed his day. On whether such utterances are to be blamed or palliated he refuses to dwell: he declines the half-evasive apology that treats the prayers against enemies as predictions rather than petitions, observes that these words show the same temper as those, and concludes that while we may give thanks for a higher law and a higher example we are not called on to apportion praise or blame, but to reverence, to sympathise and to be silent.

Keil and Delitzsch supply the reason the curse assumes, that life has never been a blessing. On the man who brought the tidings, Gill observes that the word usually means good news, and is the word used when the birth that mattered most was announced; to curse a man who did a right and acceptable thing, and was perhaps a good man, he calls more foolish and sinful still. He reports and dismisses an opinion that the prophet knew the messenger to have been Pashur. Clarke notes an old English version rendering the man child as a knave child, that being then the ordinary word for a man or servant. Ellicott finds the cruelty in the memory: the joy of the parents at the birth was needed, as in the irony of destiny, to sharpen the present misery, the crown of sorrow being the remembrance of happier days. Calvin adds a second charge, that the prophet is ungrateful toward men as well as God, the messenger having deserved nothing but thanks.
16:
The cities overthrown are identified without hesitation. Gill names Sodom and Gomorrah, utterly destroyed and never recovered, and notes that two ancient versions add in his fury; Wesley names them too. Ellicott confirms it from the verb, which is the one used in the account of their destruction, and observes that they had already become for men the standing instances of both evil and its punishment. Keil and Delitzsch take the phrase rendered repented not adverbially, without feeling compunction for the destruction, that is without pity, and read the following clause as a picture of a town besieged and suddenly taken, the one word being the wailing of the afflicted townspeople and the other the war cry of the enemies breaking in. Ellicott distinguishes the same two. Clarke reduces it to a sentence, that the man is to be in continual alarms.

Calvin measures the escalation and does not like it. The prophet mingles heaven and earth, and had it been in his power while the frenzy possessed him he would have disturbed all the elements. What follows is worse: he imprecates on an innocent man the destruction of the cities of the plain, and not a temporal punishment but endless perdition, as though asking that God be angry without showing mercy and prove wholly implacable. Had he been speaking of an inveterate enemy he should still have kept within the bounds prescribed to all the children of God; but he had nothing against the man who carried the news to his father. Calvin adds a small observation about the night: terror comes in darkness, since what happens by day we enquire into and are not so frightened, whereas a noise in the night takes full possession of us, which makes the wish for perpetual disquiet the more monstrous. The lesson he draws is practical, that we should restrain our feelings in due time, since indulged they pass all bounds and break out into fury as here.

Who was to have slain him is disputed. Gill reports three answers, that God did not, or the angel of death did not, or the messenger did not, and prefers the last, so that the man is cursed for not committing murder, and murder of an innocent infant at that. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same conclusion on grammatical grounds, that logically the subject of the verb can only be the man on whom the curse falls, and gloss the phrase as while yet in the womb, so that the mother would have become the grave. Ellicott declines to smooth the passage: the wish is uttered in strange bold language, and thought, structure and even grammar are alike, in their abruptness and irregularity, significant of intense emotion.

On the last verse Calvin gives his own rendering, offering an alternative for the conjunction in two places and translating the close as, for what purpose has this been, that from the womb I came forth to see labour and sorrow, and my days are spent in shame. He then refuses the excuse. The prophet was created to sorrow and trouble, which is the condition of all, so that God is not to be blamed; his days were spent in reproach, but there was nothing new in that, many who had an honourable testimony from God having suffered wrongs and reproaches, and he might have looked to them as examples and borne his own with patience. Gill calls the wish a sign of a fretful and impatient spirit and a carnal frame; Clarke states it flatly, that it would have been well had he never been born, since he had comfort neither in his life nor in his work.
